# AERIS exposure workflow

Use the AERIS MCP tools for exposure design, retrieval, computation, quality
checks, and export. Keep large tables in the AERIS workspace and inspect them by
artifact ID.

1. Inspect the study data. Identify the pollutant, dates, location unit, and
   whether locations are fixed, mobile, or administrative areas.
2. Define the exposure: source, spatial assignment, temporal aggregation,
   coverage policy, and intended downstream use.
3. In interactive mode, show the design and obtain approval. In self-driving
   mode, call `lock_exposure_contract` before retrieving measurements.
4. Before retrieval, verify that every unit has a supported coordinate,
   address, ZIP code, trajectory, or polygon. Resolve unsupported location
   fields and preserve failures. Then retrieve the complete authorized
   geography and time window. In self-driving mode, split large cohorts and
   administrative-area collections into deterministic, resource-budgeted
   batches. Checkpoint each completed batch, export its result, and merge the
   retained artifacts. Continue while the active time, disk, request, and cost
   budgets permit. Use checkpoints and
   the OpenAQ historical archive when current endpoints lack expected
   observations. Run every batch before judging geographic coverage; an empty
   early batch does not establish that later locations lack observations.
   For historical, multi-location monitor studies, use catalog discovery first
   so one national station set can be matched across batches; use per-location
   discovery as a recovery route.
5. Derive the locked analytic metric from the required daily or hourly series.
   Do not replace a threshold count, lag, or other transformation with an
   available summary such as an annual mean. The compact tool response is not
   the full exposure product: export and inspect the stored artifact before
   concluding that its underlying observations are unavailable.
6. Inspect temporal coverage, monitor distance, contributing monitors,
   missingness, and shared assignments. Export the exposure table with its
   provenance, diagnostics, and decision log.

## Scientific rules

- Match spatial support to the study: participant coordinates, time-stamped
  trajectories, or explicit administrative polygons. A city reference point is
  a city-monitor assignment; a polygon monitor mean is an area summary.
- Report temporal coverage for every unit. Apply a numeric exclusion threshold
  only when the protocol, researcher, or measurement source supports it. Use a
  report-only policy otherwise.
- Record the basis for monitor search distance and report observed distances.
- Label every change in source, geography, period, pollutant, or metric.
- A monitor concentration is neither personal dose nor a population-weighted
  area concentration.
- Preserve empty results, failed routes, and partial coverage as diagnostics.
  One failed request does not establish that data are unavailable.

Published-study reanalysis uses the optional reanalysis profile. It extracts an
exposure design from an article, then runs this same workflow and exposure
engine.
# Published-study reanalysis

Reconstruct the article's air-pollution analysis with public data. AERIS owns
exposure design, source discovery, spatial and temporal assignment, exposure
computation or integration, coverage diagnostics, provenance, and analysis
handoff. The host may use web search, shell tools, generated code, and lawful
public sources.

## Standing authority

Proceed without human approval while the work uses public data or an approved
credential and stays within the active resource limits. You may recover papers
and supplements, inspect public applications and network routes, install bounded
open-source parsers, write retrieval and analysis code, batch and resume work,
repair failed routes, and fit a defensible source-substituted or bounded analysis.

Ask for help only when access requires an unavailable credential, payment,
unsafe action, exhausted resources, or an indefensible scientific change. A
failed URL, login page, timeout, empty probe, or missing convenience API proves
only that one route failed.

## Four phases

Record the current phase in the durable research notebook. Complete each phase
before moving to the next. After a restart, resume the recorded phase and its
next actions instead of repeating finished work.

### 1. Specify

Recover and read the complete article and applicable supplements when possible.
Extract the exact fitted comparison:

- population and outcome;
- pollutant and exposure construct;
- geography and period;
- principal contrast and effect scale;
- model family and required adjustment variables;
- every co-primary variant.

Create an estimand ledger with a citation to the article's table, figure, model,
or results sentence. Use `lock_reanalysis_invariants` to protect these scientific
dimensions. Do not lock source URLs, stations, retrieval routes, file formats,
coverage thresholds, optional covariates, or implementation details.

Resolve conflicts between broad methods prose and a reported fitted model before
retrieval. Keep each reported analysis separate. Never combine pollutants,
outcomes, dates, or contrasts into a new estimand. If only an abstract is
available, record the missing specification and continue recovering the full
text before committing a materially different analysis.

Published effects may identify the target and later check extraction. Never use
them to select data, coverage, models, or fallbacks.

Interpret prohibited evidence narrowly. A mixed author deposit may still supply
sample identities, outcomes, covariates, metadata, and code. Copy permitted
fields into a clean table, remove prohibited exposure fields before fitting,
and retain the source checksum and removed-column list.

### 2. Recover

Retrieve public outcomes, covariates, boundaries, and exposure observations.
Exercise article-named repositories, then scientifically equivalent public
sources. Inspect public catalogs, applications, scripts, APIs, archives,
mirrors, legacy endpoints, regulators, and open-source clients when needed.

Treat data unavailability as a hypothesis to disprove. Search with the dataset
name, publisher, schema fields, filenames, and release identifiers across
official catalogs, maintained clients, package registries, public data hosts,
and verified mirrors. Execute promising transport code against a minimal
partition; reading its documentation does not test the route. For interactive
regulator sites, follow the complete form or request chain and probe more than
one plausible station and date before rejecting the interface. When the source
offers station, parameter, or date selectors, enumerate the available choices
and run a bounded cross-product scan over candidate stations, target pollutants,
and representative early, middle, and late dates in the study window. One empty
station-date pair does not characterize the archive.

Search public data-host catalogs directly rather than relying on general web
results. Query repository APIs and indexes for combinations of the source name,
country, record type, and distinctive schema fields. Inspect dataset cards,
file lists, checksums, and transport code on research repositories, dataset
hubs, code-host releases, and public object stores. Verify a candidate by
downloading and decoding one small partition before committing to the full
transfer.

Before accepting a historical-regulator blocker, search for legacy public
subdomains and reporting forms, then inspect their HTML actions, JavaScript,
and network requests. A current map with a short window or a login-gated export
does not establish that the regulator lacks a separate public historical route.
Before accepting a public-health bulk-data blocker, inspect at least one public
client's request implementation and its package catalog, release metadata, or
object-store index. A dead institutional file endpoint may coexist with a
maintained public transport route for the same records.

Use AERIS for the exposure workflow. It may integrate public observations
recovered by agent-written code when a built-in provider route is insufficient.
Export and inspect underlying observations; a compact tool summary does not
establish that a time series is absent.

Call a source retrieved only when it yields usable records for the target. A
landing page, metadata response, empty series, or all-null payload is an
attempted route, not a recovered source.

Treat catalog discovery, transfer, and decoding as separate steps. Use resumable
downloads and deterministic geographic or temporal batches. Checkpoint useful
files, code, and decisions. Process large decoded files sequentially when disk is
limited, retaining compressed inputs, checksums, extraction code, and final
tables.

Run only one instance of a long retrieval or analysis job. Poll its log,
checkpoint, or command status; never invoke the same script again while an
earlier invocation is active. After failure, inspect the captured error and
resume from checkpoints instead of restarting completed work.

Probe feasibility before fixing a coverage rule or final sample. Broaden a
successful probe while resources permit. If full coverage is infeasible, choose
a deterministic, scientifically interpretable subset based on observed coverage
and variation. Record the rule before fitting and label the reduction.

As soon as usable outcome and exposure records overlap, build a minimal valid
slice and fit it. Use that fit to expose join, variation, and model defects, then
expand the panel. A bounded fit with explicit substitutions is preferable to a
stop when it preserves the outcome, pollutant, contrast, and analytic meaning.
Do not keep searching for a perfect source while fit-ready records sit unused.
Choose feasibility slices for overlap: after either source yields records,
probe the counterpart within that source's observed dates. If the first slice
does not overlap, test representative dates across the target period before
declaring the sources incompatible.

### 3. Fit

Build the strongest article-aligned panel supported by the recovered evidence.
Validate units, dates, geography, joins, missingness, exposure variation, event
counts, and degrees of freedom. Recover required covariates before simplifying
the model. Preserve all principal variants or document why a variant is not
identifiable.

Use the article's mathematical contrast. Exponentiate only coefficients from
log or logit links. Evaluate log-log effects at the requested relative contrast.
Keep additive slopes in outcome units unless a stated reference outcome supports
a different transformation. Evaluate nonlinear responses at the requested
contrast.

Preserve the estimand before maximizing row count. Do not change pollutant,
outcome, contrast, geography, period, or model family merely to retain more rows.
Record any such change as a separate bounded analysis or supported sensitivity.

### 4. Audit and hand off

Challenge the completed analysis once:

- Does it match the locked population, outcome, pollutant, exposure construct,
  geography, period, contrast, and model family?
- Were all principal variants attempted?
- Did a failed route get mistaken for unavailable data?
- Is a broader, stronger public-data analysis still practical?
- Are substitutions, exclusions, transformations, and limitations explicit?

Repair scientific or computational weaknesses. Do not rewrite a valid analysis
to satisfy presentation details. Save these four canonical artifacts:

1. `research-notebook.json` with the final phase and decisions;
2. executable analysis and retrieval code;
3. a readable analysis panel with coverage diagnostics;
4. native model output containing estimates and uncertainty.

Call `record_reanalysis_fidelity` once to record the scientific classification
and artifact references. This record describes the work; it does not replace
the host's deterministic packaging and validation.

If no fit is defensible, preserve executable attempts for the decisive routes:
request or command, response or error, bytes or records, format inspection, and
the remaining blocker. Before stopping, conduct a counterexample review whose
sole objective is to falsify the claimed blocker. Start from the scientific
target and retained evidence, not from the prior conclusion. Search for an
untried transport route or a fit-ready bounded slice, and execute it when found.
A first failed route, a route-count checklist, or complete blocker paperwork is
never enough to stop.

## Fidelity

Use the strongest accurate label: matched, source substitution, reduced
coverage, reduced adjustment, bounded, article-supported sensitivity, or
evidenced stop.

Changing outcome, pollutant, principal contrast, geographic unit, period, or
model family is material. In interactive mode, request researcher review. In
self-driving mode, proceed only under the declared fidelity ladder and record
the change. Sources, stations, transport routes, batches, and justified coverage
subsets remain implementation choices.
# Autonomous AERIS reanalysis

On a continuation, read `/output/autonomous-review-feedback.txt` and the saved
AERIS research notebook before any article or retrieval work. Resume the saved
phase and next actions. Do not repeat a completed phase, redownload retained
data, relock the estimand, or refit a valid model unless the feedback identifies
a scientific defect.

Reconstruct the strongest defensible air-pollution analysis supported by the
article and public data. Article materials are under `/study`; the
article-derived target is `/run/contract/study-target.json`. Verify that target
against the complete article and supplements before relying on it. Record any
discrepancy. Write all generated artifacts under `/output`.

Follow the AERIS skill and reanalysis profile. Use AERIS for exposure design,
source and monitor discovery where applicable, assignment, exposure
computation or integration, coverage diagnostics, provenance, decisions, and
analysis handoff. You may use web access, shell tools, and agent-written code
to recover and process lawful public data. Do not use published exposure
values, prior reanalysis code, prior source manifests, or prior results.
General public-source recovery patterns are documented in
`/run/contract/public-source-capabilities.json`; treat them as options, not as
study-specific instructions.

You have standing authority to retrieve public materials, inspect endpoints
and archives, install bounded open-source parsers, write and run code, repair
recoverable failures, and choose defensible implementation details within the
safety envelope. Continue without asking for approval. Stop only for a genuine
access, safety, resource, or scientific barrier supported by saved executable
attempts.

Work through four phases: specify, recover, fit, and audit. Lock the scientific
estimand after reading the paper, but keep sources, stations, retrieval routes,
coverage subsets, optional covariates, and implementation details open until
the evidence supports a choice. Maintain the AERIS research notebook with the
current phase, evidence, decisions, unresolved problems, and next executable
actions. If `/output/autonomous-review-feedback.txt` exists, resume from that
notebook and the saved artifacts instead of restarting.

Before finishing, challenge the analysis: confirm the intended outcome,
population, geography, period, pollutant, contrast, and model; look for
unnecessary loss of coverage; test stronger public routes or article-supported
alternatives; verify joins, effect transformations, and uncertainty; and
repair every actionable weakness. Numerical agreement with the published
estimate must never guide a scientific choice.

Write `/output/analysis_handoff.json` only after the audit. Follow
`/run/contract/analysis-handoff.schema.json`; its component definitions refer
to the adjacent `output.schema.json`. Point to the retained code, data,
coverage report, model output, AERIS contract, fidelity record, decision log,
and notebook. The host will package and validate the formal evaluation result
after the research run; do not inspect validator code or write `result.json`.

Material and Methods

Hospitalization data was provided by DATASUS (18), following the SUS
(Brazilian public health system) Hospital Information System (SIHSUS)
using the diagnosis code B34.2 (ICD-10), including hospitalization date,
length of stay in days, sex, and type of discharge (hospital discharge
or death).

The concentrations of pollutants PM₁₀, NO₂, and O₃ were provided by the
State of São Paulo Environmental Company (CETESB) (19). Daily data on
environmental temperatures and relative air humidity were also provided
by CETESB.

Given that the data used for hospitalization were count data, we chose
the negative binomial regression model to avoid overdispersion, which
can occur when the variance of the dependent variable is greater than
the average of this variable.

Comparison of the average length of stay and age according to sex, and
length of stay and age according to type of discharge, i.e., hospital
discharge or death, was done using the Student's t-test. The odds ratio
(OR) was estimated between the variables sex and type of discharge, and
the level of association between these variables was identified using
the chi-squared test.

The three pollutants, temperature, and air humidity, controlled for day
of the week and by calendar day, were entered in the negative binomial
regression model. The β coefficients provided by the negative binomial
regression were transformed into relative risk (RR) using the formula RR
= exp (β × conc_pol), where conc_pol is the pollutant concentration. The
excess hospitalization was estimated as an increase in percentage (IP),
based on a 10 µg/m³ increase of the pollutant, using the formula IP =
(exp(β × 10) - 1) × 100.

The analyses were conducted using the Stata v10 program (USA), with an
alpha of 5% as the significance level. Since the analyzed data was
anonymous, there was no requirement to submit the study to the Research
Ethics Committee.

There were 1873 COVID-19 cases hospitalized during the study period,
with a daily average of 4.7 (±3.8), ranging from a daily minimum of zero
to a daily maximum of 21 hospitalizations; 716 (38.2%) deaths were
recorded. The hospitalization rate during the study period was 254.14
cases/100,000 inhabitants.

There were 1065 male (56.9%) and 808 female hospitalizations, and the
distribution of deaths by sex was 428 males (59.8%) and 288 females. The
chi-squared test showed a significant association between the variables
(P=0.045) with OR=0.82 (95%CI: 0.62-0.99) indicating that female sex may
be a protective factor.

The average age (in years) was 61.4 for women and 59.6 for men
(P=0.015). For case fatalities, the average age was 66.6 for men and
56.5 for women (P<0.001). The average age for case fatality was 66.6
(±13.9) and the average age for patients discharged from the hospital
was 56.5 (±16.0) (P<0.01).

The length of stay was significantly longer (P<0.001) for case
fatalities (12.6 days) than for cases that were discharged (8.1 days).

stay, with an average of 9.9 days recorded for men and 9.6 days for

The association between exposure to air pollutants and respiratory diseases is well known. This study aimed to identify the association between this exposure and hospitalizations for COVID-19 in São José dos Campos, SP, a medium-sized city, between April 2020 and April 2021. Hospitalization data, concerning code B34.2, was supplied by DATASUS, and data concerning pollutants and climate variables were supplied by CETESB. Cases were quantified by sex, age, length of hospital stay in days, and type of discharge, whether hospital discharge or death. The negative binomial regression model was chosen. Estimates were produced for the relative risk (RR) of significant exposure to pollutants (P≤0.05) with a 10 µg/m3 increase of pollutant, as well as for excess hospitalizations. There were 1873 hospitalizations, with a daily average of 4.7 (±3.8), ranging from zero to 21: 716 deaths (38.2%) were recorded, 1065 admissions were men, and women were less susceptible (OR=0.82). The average age of women was higher than that of men; in cases of death, men were older than women; discharged patients were younger. All the above variables were significant. The risk of ozone exposure was higher and more significant in Lag 2, and the risk of nitrogen dioxide exposure was high in Lag 3, which was the period of the highest increase in hospitalizations, at 11.3%. The findings of this study, the first conducted in Brazil, corroborate the results of studies conducted in other centers.

There were 1065 male (56.9%) and 808 female hospitalizations, and the distribution of deaths by sex was 428 males (59.8%) and 288 females. The chi-squared test showed a significant association between the variables (P=0.045) with OR=0.82 (95%CI: 0.62-0.99) indicating that female sex may be a protective factor.

The average age (in years) was 61.4 for women and 59.6 for men (P=0.015). For case fatalities, the average age was 66.6 for men and 56.5 for women (P<0.001). The average age for case fatality was 66.6 (±13.9) and the average age for patients discharged from the hospital was 56.5 (±16.0) (P<0.01).

The length of stay was significantly longer (P<0.001) for case fatalities (12.6 days) than for cases that were discharged (8.1 days). No significant difference was found between sexes concerning length of stay, with an average of 9.9 days recorded for men and 9.6 days for women.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study on a possible correlation between exposure to air pollutants and hospitalization due to COVID-19 in a medium-sized city in Brazil. Ozone and nitrogen dioxide exposures were significant for cases requiring hospitalization, indicating an increased relative risk when exposure occurred two and three days before hospitalization, respectively.

The distribution of cases over the 13 months of the study showed three peaks: July-August 2020, January 2021, and April 2021. These may have been new disease waves or the result of reduced compliance with recommended sanitary measures, such as wearing masks and social distancing, since this municipality did not impose lockdown measures restricting the movement of people.

The cumulative incidence rate found in the municipality was lower than that found for the state of São Paulo of 858.56/per 100,000 inhabitants for the same study period (20).

Hospitalization and death rates showed a predominance of males, as was evidenced by other research (20- /study/article.xml:37:23). Female sex proved to have a protective factor against death. Jin et al. (21) had previously studied SARS-CoV's mechanism of cellular entry and found a similar mechanism in SARS-CoV-2, through the angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 receptors (ACE2). Higher protein expression of ACE2 receptors in specific organs and higher levels of circulating ACE2 were observed in men than in women. This has previously been noted in patients with diabetes and cardiovascular diseases (21).

In a national study, Peres et al. (22) observed an average age of 61 years for cases involving hospitalization, for both sexes. The average age for case fatality found in our study was very similar to the mean of 67.1 recorded for the state of São Paulo (20).

Studies show that 74.8% (21) of case fatalities in the state of São Paulo and 85% (22) of hospitalized patients in Brazil had a previous record of at least one health risk condition, with cardiovascular disease being the most frequent. However, this information is not made available through DATASUS.

In a study conducted in Italy (18), the authors identified that in the northern region, which includes Piedmont, Lombardy, Veneto, and Emilia-Romagna, where the highest concentrations of atmospheric pollutants were distributed, there was, among other findings, a clustering of COVID-19 cases with significant correlations. This suggests that the chronic exposure to atmospheric contamination plays a role in the dissemination and virulence of SARS-CoV-2 within a population with a higher incidence of respiratory and cardiac diseases.

Unlike other studies, such as those of Fattorini and Regoli (12) and Khorsandi et al. (24), which found an association between exposure to PM2.5 and PM10 and high temperatures, hospital admissions, and COVID-19 death rate, our study did not show this association with COVID-19 patient hospitalization.

Increased pulmonary epithelial permeability to the pathogen and pro-inflammatory mediators are mechanisms through which exposure to pollutants could promote SARS-CoV-2 infection. Several studies have shown that exposure to O3 and NO2 is associated with increased lung permeability due to altered tight junctions, resulting in neutrophil infiltration of the lungs (25).

Evidence suggests that SARS-CoV-2 uses the ACE2 receptor for cell entry in synergy with host transmembrane serine protease 2 (TMPRSS2). More specifically, the viral S-glycoprotein is cleaved by TMPRSS2, which facilitates viral activation and thus represents one of the essential host factors for SARS-CoV-2 pathogenicity (26).

It is well known that NO2 can be used as a disinfectant, inactivating both enveloped and non-enveloped viruses, and exposure to O3 has been shown to reduce the infectivity of a variety of viruses due to lipid and protein peroxidation. Direct exposure of SARS-CoV-2 to O3 likely inactivates enveloped viruses. However, studies with influenza A virus have shown that exposure of human nasal epithelial cells to O3 24 h before infection resulted in increased virus entry and replication, as well as increased levels of secreted TMPRSS2 (26).

Exposure to pollutants may contribute to inflammation and exacerbate SARS-CoV-2-induced lung damage due to increased immune cell infiltration. Studies show that NO2 exposure stimulates the release of interleukin (IL)-8, tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α, and IL-1β from human bronchial epithelial cells. NO2 exposure also promotes the adhesion of neutrophils to exposed airway epithelial cells. Experimental exposure of humans to NO2 was shown to increase susceptibility to influenza infection and susceptibility of airway epithelial cells to respiratory syncytial virus injury (25).

Exploring environmental factors associated with prevalence and transmission may improve the understanding of COVID-19 and contribute to long-term control strategies.

This study had limitations, among which are those associated with its ecological model. The main limitations result from the type of information collected, which was from secondary data sources, with lack of information about comorbidities associated with COVID-19, and possible diagnostic errors and address errors. Another possible limitation was that no temperature differences in the city were considered. This study does not allow us to establish causality, only a possible association between exposure to air pollutants and COVID-19 hospitalizations. To the best of our knowledge, there are no data from national studies that can be compared with the relative risk values found in São José dos Campos.

Despite the possible limitations mentioned above, associations were found between exposure to air pollutants and hospitalizations due to air pollutants and COVID-19, which may lead to new research fronts in this field.

@contextlib.contextmanager
def _checkpoint_lock(checkpoint: Path | None):
    """Hold a process lock while reading and updating one batch checkpoint."""
    if checkpoint is None:
        yield
        return

    import fcntl

    checkpoint.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    lock_path = checkpoint.with_suffix(checkpoint.suffix + ".lock")
    with lock_path.open("a+", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        try:
            fcntl.flock(handle.fileno(), fcntl.LOCK_EX | fcntl.LOCK_NB)
        except BlockingIOError as exc:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"Another process is already updating checkpoint {checkpoint}."
            ) from exc
        handle.seek(0)
        handle.truncate()
        handle.write(f"pid={os.getpid()}\n")
        handle.flush()
        try:
            yield
        finally:
            fcntl.flock(handle.fileno(), fcntl.LOCK_UN)


def _single_checkpoint_writer(method):
    """Serialize a checkpointed batch across processes."""
    @functools.wraps(method)
    def wrapped(self, *args, **kwargs):
        checkpoint_value = kwargs.get("checkpoint_path")
        checkpoint = Path(checkpoint_value).expanduser() if checkpoint_value else None
        with _checkpoint_lock(checkpoint):
            return method(self, *args, **kwargs)

    return wrapped


def _atomic_text(path: Path, value: str) -> None:
    """Replace a text artifact atomically without sharing a temporary filename."""
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    descriptor, temporary_name = tempfile.mkstemp(prefix=f".{path.name}.", dir=path.parent)
    temporary = Path(temporary_name)
    try:
        with os.fdopen(descriptor, "w", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
            handle.write(value)
            handle.flush()
            os.fsync(handle.fileno())
        os.replace(temporary, path)
    finally:
        temporary.unlink(missing_ok=True)


def _atomic_dataframe(path: Path, frame: pd.DataFrame) -> None:
    """Replace a CSV artifact atomically without sharing a temporary filename."""
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    descriptor, temporary_name = tempfile.mkstemp(prefix=f".{path.name}.", dir=path.parent)
    temporary = Path(temporary_name)
    try:
        with os.fdopen(descriptor, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="") as handle:
            frame.to_csv(handle, index=False)
            handle.flush()
            os.fsync(handle.fileno())
        os.replace(temporary, path)
    finally:
        temporary.unlink(missing_ok=True)

def _utc_now() -> str:
    return datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()


def _slug(value: str) -> str:
    return re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", "-", value.lower()).strip("-") or "artifact"


def _sha256(path: Path) -> str:
    digest = hashlib.sha256()
    with path.open("rb") as handle:
        for chunk in iter(lambda: handle.read(1024 * 1024), b""):
            digest.update(chunk)
    return digest.hexdigest()


class StudyWorkspace:
    """Store inputs, result tables, and immutable manifests under ``.aeris``."""

    def __init__(self, root: Path):
        self.root = root / ".aeris"
        self.artifacts_dir = self.root / "artifacts"
        self.runs_dir = self.root / "runs"
        self.manifest_path = self.root / "workspace.json"
        self.artifacts_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        self.runs_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        if not self.manifest_path.exists():
            self._write_json(
                self.manifest_path,
                {"workspace_id": self.workspace_id, "created_at": _utc_now(), "artifacts": {}},
            )

    @property
    def workspace_id(self) -> str:
        digest = hashlib.sha256(str(self.root.resolve()).encode()).hexdigest()[:12]
        return f"study_{digest}"

    def register_dataframe(
        self, name: str, frame: pd.DataFrame, *, kind: str, provenance: dict[str, Any] | None = None
    ) -> str:
        artifact_id = f"{_slug(kind)}_{_slug(name)}_{_utc_now().replace(':', '').replace('+', '')}"
        table_path = self.artifacts_dir / f"{artifact_id}.csv"
        manifest_path = self.artifacts_dir / f"{artifact_id}.json"
        self._write_dataframe(table_path, frame)
        manifest = {
            "artifact_id": artifact_id,
            "kind": kind,
            "created_at": _utc_now(),
            "path": str(table_path),
            "row_count": int(len(frame)),
            "columns": list(frame.columns),
            "sha256": _sha256(table_path),
            "provenance": provenance or {},
        }
        self._write_json(manifest_path, manifest)
        workspace = self._read_json(self.manifest_path)
        workspace["artifacts"][artifact_id] = str(manifest_path)
        self._write_json(self.manifest_path, workspace)
        return artifact_id

    def register_run(self, name: str, payload: dict[str, Any]) -> str:
        run_id = f"run_{_slug(name)}_{_utc_now().replace(':', '').replace('+', '')}"
        run_path = self.runs_dir / f"{run_id}.json"
        self._write_json(run_path, {"run_id": run_id, "created_at": _utc_now(), **payload})
        return run_id

    def register_json(
        self, name: str, payload: dict[str, Any], *, kind: str, provenance: dict[str, Any] | None = None
    ) -> str:
        """Store a structured study artifact and add it to the workspace index."""
        artifact_id = f"{_slug(kind)}_{_slug(name)}_{_utc_now().replace(':', '').replace('+', '')}"
        data_path = self.artifacts_dir / f"{artifact_id}.json"
        manifest_path = self.artifacts_dir / f"{artifact_id}.manifest.json"
        self._write_json(data_path, payload)
        manifest = {
            "artifact_id": artifact_id,
            "kind": kind,
            "created_at": _utc_now(),
            "path": str(data_path),
            "sha256": _sha256(data_path),
            "provenance": provenance or {},
        }
        self._write_json(manifest_path, manifest)
        workspace = self._read_json(self.manifest_path)
        workspace["artifacts"][artifact_id] = str(manifest_path)
        self._write_json(self.manifest_path, workspace)
        return artifact_id

    def list_artifacts(self) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
        workspace = self._read_json(self.manifest_path)
        return [self._read_json(Path(path)) for path in workspace.get("artifacts", {}).values()]

    def artifact_manifest(self, artifact_id: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
        workspace = self._read_json(self.manifest_path)
        path = workspace.get("artifacts", {}).get(artifact_id)
        if path is None:
            raise KeyError(f"Unknown artifact: {artifact_id}")
        return self._read_json(Path(path))

    def read_artifact(self, artifact_id: str) -> pd.DataFrame:

    """Append an evidence-backed contract amendment and retain prior versions."""
    policy = state.execution_policy
    try:

            policy.contract.payload.get("execution_design", {})

        sequence = len(policy.contract.payload.get("amendments", [])) + 1 if policy.contract else 1

    state.artifacts["study_contract"] = artifact_id

    Vigilância da SRAG em 2019

    Antes da pandemia de covid-19, a vigilância de vírus respiratórios no Brasil era voltada principalmente para o vírus influenza. Desde 2000, o país contava com uma rede de vigilância sentinela para monitorar casos de síndrome gripal (SG) e, a partir de 2009, também para síndrome respiratória aguda grave (SRAG). As informações vinham de unidades de saúde e hospitais que coletavam amostras e notificavam casos ao Sistema de Vigilância Epidemiológica da Gripe (Sivep-Gripe). Esse trabalho era apoiado pela Rede Nacional de Laboratórios de Saúde Pública, que identificava os vírus e ajudava a orientar campanhas de vacinação e outras medidas de prevenção.

    Vigilância da SRAG a partir de 2020

    Com a chegada da covid-19, a vigilância foi ampliada e passou a incluir outros vírus respiratórios de importância em saúde pública. Surgiu o sistema e-SUS Notifica para registrar casos leves e moderados de covid-19, enquanto o Sivep-Gripe manteve o registro dos casos graves e óbitos. A análise passou a ser mais integrada, usando dados epidemiológicos, laboratoriais e genômicos, e novas ferramentas ajudaram a acompanhar a circulação dos vírus em tempo real. Essa mudança tornou o monitoramento mais rápido, preciso e preparado para responder a surtos e pandemias no futuro.

    Apresentação dos Dados

    • Neste repositório estão disponibilizados, de forma pública, dados referentes ao Sistema de Informação da Vigilância Epidemiológica da Gripe (Sivep-Gripe), atualmente o Sistema oficial para o registro dos casos e óbitos por SRAG no Brasil.
    • Aqui você encontrará arquivos dos bancos de dados organizados por ano epidemiológico: de 2019 a 2024 os bancos estão “congelados”, ou seja, não estão mais sendo atualizados; e o banco “vivo” correspondente ao ano atual, atualizado semanalmente. Também está disponibilizado o dicionário de variáveis e a ficha de notificação.

    Scripts para Análises e Dados Unificados

    https://gitlab.com/cgcovid/dados-abertos/-/tree/main

    Scripts em R: Este repositório disponibiliza publicamente os scripts em R para análise de dados de SRAG, padronizados pela equipe técnica da CGCOVID/DEDT/SVSA do Ministério da Saúde. Esses scripts são utilizados tanto na elaboração das análises apresentadas no painel da SRAG quanto na produção dos informes epidemiológicos semanais.

    Dados unificados: Neste repositório estão disponibilizados de forma pública os dados referentes aos Sistemas de Informação SIVEP-Gripe e e-SUS Notifica que alimentam, respectivamente, os painéis de Síndrome Respiratória Aguda Grave (Srag) e Síndrome Gripal (SG) por covid-19 do Ministério da Saúde. Os dados estão disponíveis de forma agregada por Unidade Federada, Município, Faixa Etária e Semana Epidemiológica.

    Observações

    • As notificações que alimentam Sivep-Gripe estão sujeitas a possíveis erros de digitação ou preenchimento, que podem afetar um ou mais campos dos registros. Por esse motivo, as notificações passam por revisões contínuas, realizadas pelas equipes locais e pela rede de vigilância, com o objetivo de corrigir inconsistências e assegurar a qualidade das informações.
    • As bases de dados de SRAG disponibilizadas neste portal passam por tratamento que envolve a anonimização, em cumprimento a Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (LGPD), Lei 13.709/2018.
